title: Nonviolence
hookLine: a pope's peace message names active nonviolence as a way of life and of politics

cards: A kitchen, late at night, two people mid-argument. One voice rises. The other has a choice: rise to meet it, go cold and silent, or try something harder.
Paul names that harder thing for the Christians in Rome, in the Douay-Rheims: "Be not overcome by evil: but overcome evil by good." Not run from it. Not match it.
Overcome it, with its opposite. Pope Francis built a World Day of Peace message around one word, and carried it from kitchens like that one all the way into politics. Today, nonviolence.

teach.h: LOVE YOUR ENEMIES, DO THEM GOOD.
teach.b: Francis starts with the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus says to love your enemies, and in the Douay-Rheims, "do good to them that hate you."
Francis reads that as a whole way of living: to be a true follower of Jesus today includes embracing his teaching about nonviolence.
Then the word that matters most: active. Nonviolence isn't giving up, looking away, or letting a bully win. It's a choice to resist evil without copying it.
Francis names people who did exactly that and changed things, among them Mother Teresa and Martin Luther King. It takes courage, planning and nerve. It can stand in a street.
Where does it begin? Not first at a border or a parliament.
At home, Francis says, in families, where people learn to argue without wounding and to forgive without pretending nothing happened. A kitchen table is a peace table too. And an honest note.
The Catechism still keeps a place for legitimate defense, and Catholic teaching thinks hard about when force can be just.

Francis doesn't erase that. He asks that nonviolence become the first instinct and the normal style, in private life and in politics, with force a last and sorrowful exception. Two strands, held in one Church.
Up close, it looks small: an angry reply left unsent, a voice lowered, standing beside someone instead of against them.

how: Catholics pray for peace at Mass and on the Church's World Day of Peace, and some Catholic groups train in nonviolent action; parish and family life is where the Church asks it to begin.

o: resisting evil actively, without using its weapons
staying out of every conflict to keep the peace
giving in quietly so a fight ends sooner

s: in Francis's message, nonviolence means doing nothing
he calls it active: resisting evil without copying it, which takes courage.
the message roots nonviolence in Jesus' own teaching
it goes back to the Sermon on the Mount: love your enemies, do good to them that hate you.
the Catechism has no place for self-defense
it keeps a place for legitimate defense; Francis asks that nonviolence be the first instinct.

games.q: a coworker mocks you in a meeting, in front of everyone. what fits the active nonviolence of Francis's message?
o: stay calm, name what happened, and talk to them after.
say nothing, ever, and let it go on.
games.why: active nonviolence is neither revenge nor looking away. it resists the wrong without copying it: overcome evil by good.

practice: Bring to mind one conflict you're in right now, with a coworker, a sibling, a neighbor, a thread online, and notice what you're holding ready: the sharp line you've rehearsed, the silence meant to punish.
Without giving up what's true, find the gentler move, a question instead of a verdict, and breathe with it. If you pray, bring that person before God by name.

wordCard.voice: Nonviolence. Resisting evil without copying it: in Francis's message, a style for home and for politics, rooted in the Sermon on the Mount.

carryVoice: Your line: active nonviolence. Not passive, not violent: overcome evil by good. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Be not overcome by evil: but overcome evil by good.
